So you asked me when I knew, and honestly there was no big moment. I swam for eleven years. I made two national finals and I have never once been able to explain to a normal person what four thirty in the morning does to you. The turning point was not dramatic. I got to the pool one Tuesday, I sat on the edge, and I did not want to get in. That was it. I have not raced since that day and I have not missed it as much as everybody warned me I would. What I do miss is the intensity. Nothing since has asked that much of me, and part of me is still looking for something that will.

Everybody prepares an athlete for the decision. Almost nobody prepares them for what comes after it. I have worked with people who left at seventeen and people who left at thirty-four, and the pattern is the same in both. The first two weeks feel like a holiday. The two months after that feel like freedom. And then, somewhere around month four, the structure that ran their whole day is simply gone, and nothing has replaced it yet. That gap is where the trouble lives. So my advice has not changed in twenty years: before you stop, decide what the new demanding thing is going to be. Not what you will do instead. What will ask as much of you.
